extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, employers, SDS/label preparers, and OSHA compliance officers/stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Final-rule explanatory guidance on definitions and hazard-classification requirements under OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (HCS), including finalized wording for key defined terms and the scope of classification (labels and SDS entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of combustible dust
rubrics_metrics.description: Final definition: "finely divided solid particulates of a substance or mixture that pose a flash-fire hazard or explosion hazard when dispersed in air or other oxidizing media."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA replaced the proposed phrases "liable to catch fire" and "ignition" with "pose a flash-fire hazard" (consistent with NFPA 652/654), replaced "explode" with "explosion hazard," and changed "particles" to "particulates." OSHA explained that flammable solids are one type of combustible dust but that both hazards should be identified. OSHA declined to add confinement and particle-size criteria (e.g., <500 microns) to the HCS definition because confinement and particle size are conditions external to the intrinsic properties of the material; HCS definitions are written to capture intrinsic properties rather than the conditions required for ignition. OSHA referenced NFPA alignment and pointed readers to Appendix B.7 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarification of wording for combustible dust hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrases "liable to catch fire" and "on ignition" were eliminated; "catch fire" was replaced with "pose a flash-fire hazard."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA agreed commenters found "catch fire" insufficiently clear and adopted wording aligned with NFPA standards to improve clarity and consistency. This wording change is part of the final combustible dust definition and is intended to avoid conflation with flammable solids and to focus on the hazard rather than ambiguous phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of confinement and particle size from combustible dust definition
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA declined to include confinement and particle-size criteria (such as less than 500 microns) in the HCS definition of combustible dust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: confinement is a condition external to the material and particle size does not alone determine whether a material can ignite; HCS definitions focus on intrinsic properties. OSHA contrasted this with classification elements (e.g., flash point for flammable liquids) that are intrinsic properties. OSHA noted that confinement/particle-size are relevant to assessing ignition risk in handling/use but not to intrinsic classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of exposure or exposed
rubrics_metrics.description: Finalized to mean that an employee is subjected in the course of employment to a "hazardous chemical," rather than to "a chemical that is a physical or health hazard."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This revision clarifies that the HCS covers hazards of all hazardous chemicals, including those considered HNOCs (health- or non-classified chemicals). OSHA received no comments opposing this change and finalized it as proposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of gas, liquid, and solid
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed and is finalizing new definitions for "gas," "liquid," and "solid" to align with GHS Rev. 7, including adding equivalent degrees Fahrenheit and PSI for U.S. usage. The GHS definition of 'solid' was adopted for substances/mixtures not meeting definitions of liquid or gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA included temperature/pressure (e.g., 68 °F (20 °C) and 14.69 PSI (101.3 kPa)) in gas/liquid definitions for U.S. clarity. For viscous substances or mixtures where a specific melting point could not be determined, OSHA revised wording so that cited test methods (ASTM 4359-90 or the ADR penetrometer test) 'can establish' whether a viscous substance is a liquid — removing language implying mandatory testing. OSHA emphasized the HCS does not require testing for hazard classification and cited GHS Chapter 1.3.2.4.1 noting GHS does not impose testing requirements. OSHA expects these definitions to improve harmonization and clarity for classification and SDS/label preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No testing requirement for classification
rubrics_metrics.description: HCS specifies that there is no requirement to test a chemical for hazard classification purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarified that proposed phrasing 'shall be subjected to' implied a testing requirement and was revised; test methods may be used to establish a property but are not mandated. OSHA cited the preexisting regulatory language (48 FR 53280, 53290) and GHS provisions supporting that testing is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hazardous chemical (pyrophoric gas change)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed updating the definition of "hazardous chemical" to delete a reference to pyrophoric gas because pyrophoric gas is being classified as a physical hazard in the flammable gas hazard class (moved to Appendix B.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One commenter accepted the revision; OSHA finalized the revised definition as proposed. The change reflects reclassification of pyrophoric gas definitions into Appendix B to organize physical hazard criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of immediate outer package
rubrics_metrics.description: New definition: the immediate outer package is the first box or package surrounding the container (e.g., for a kit, the container is the vial and the immediate outer package is the first box surrounding that vial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA finalized this definition to relax labeling on small containers while requiring complete label information on the immediate outer package; commenters supported the clarification and harmonization with DOT. No opposition to the proposed definition was received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of physical hazard
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised definition noting that 'the criteria for determining whether a chemical is classified as a physical hazard are detailed in Appendix B' and moving/adjusting parentheticals (e.g., explicitly referencing aerosols and adding desensitized explosives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA finalized the revised definition with minor grammatical amendments to the parentheticals ("flammable (gases, liquids, or solids)" and "oxidizers (gases, liquids, or solids)") to improve consistency and to reflect new aerosol and desensitized explosive hazard classes in Appendix B aligned with GHS Rev. 7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of physician or other licensed health care professional (PLHCP)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA added a definition for PLHCP to replace "physician and nurse" in paragraph (i), consistent with other OSHA standards and modern medical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new PLHCP definition is consistent with how OSHA has defined the term in health standards since the 1991 bloodborne pathogen standard (29 CFR 1910.1030). Commenters agreed it reduces confusion and harmonizes across standards. OSHA finalized as proposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deletion and relocation of pyrophoric gas definition
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is deleting the definition of "pyrophoric gas" from paragraph (c) and adding it to Appendix B.2 (physical hazard criteria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change is coordinated with classifying pyrophoric gas as a physical hazard in the flammable gas hazard class; commenters accepted the change and OSHA finalized it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of released for shipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Final definition: "a chemical that has been packaged and labeled in the manner in which it will be distributed or sold."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA aligned this term with EPA's definition in 40 CFR 152.3 but did not include storage-location language used by EPA. OSHA clarified it does not intend manufacturers/importers/distributors to print the phrase "released for shipment" on labels. OSHA eliminated the proposed requirement to include a released-for-shipment date on the label, addressing commenters' concerns about confusion with business/logistics readiness. The definition is retained primarily to clarify the meaning of related labeling provisions (paragraph (f)(11)) and to ensure alignment with EPA where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on harmonization with GHS
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's policy is to align definitions with the GHS where appropriate but not to restrict HCS terms only to GHS-defined terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA noted the HCS regulatory framework predates GHS and includes additional provisions to protect workers; if OSHA uses a term not taken directly from GHS it will be transparent that the definition has not yet been harmonized and could change. OSHA declined a comment that only GHS terms should be used and explained where HCS adds definitions for worker-protective purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of hazard classification (paragraph (d)(1)) — intrinsic properties and downstream hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA finalized revised (d)(1): hazard classification shall include any hazards associated with the chemical's intrinsic properties including: (d)(1)(i) a change in the chemical's physical form; and (d)(1)(ii) chemical reaction products associated with known or reasonably anticipated uses or applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA removed the proposed phrase "under normal conditions of use and foreseeable emergencies" to avoid confusion and rephrased to articulate intent. OSHA clarified that hazards identified and classified under (d)(1)(ii) (chemical reaction products from known/anticipated uses) will not be required to appear on a product's label but must be included in Section 2 of the SDS. This change clarifies manufacturer/importer obligations to consider intrinsic hazards and certain downstream reaction products when classifying, while distinguishing label vs SDS placement. OSHA provided examples (e.g., epoxy syringes, spray foams, hair smoothing products) where downstream reactions create distinct hazards that must be communicated to downstream users via SDS content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer/importer responsibility for downstream-use hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA asserts manufacturers and importers have historically been required to identify and disclose hazards related to normal conditions of use and foreseeable emergencies, and the finalized language reaffirms their duty to ascertain and disclose chemical hazards to downstream users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA responded to stakeholder claims that HCS historically did not require classification for downstream reaction hazards by citing prior preamble language and guidance indicating manufacturers/importers must consider normal conditions of use and foreseeable emergencies. OSHA maintained the final language is a rephrasing, not a substantive expansion, and relied on previous guidance and compliance directives to support the interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from adding certain new definitions to HCS
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA declined to add definitions for terms outside the HCS scope such as "injurious corrosive material" (a term in 29 CFR 1910.151(c)) and declined to add a definition for "nanomaterials" to the HCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the HCS is not the appropriate location for definitions not used in the HCS or that fall outside the rulemaking's scope. OSHA pointed stakeholders to the relevant standards/regulators (e.g., MIOSHA, EPA) for such terms and noted particle characteristics are addressed elsewhere in Appendix D Section 9 for SDS content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for cross-standard interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the same term is used but not defined in another OSHA standard, and OSHA has guidance specific to that standard, that guidance (not the HCS definition) is the relevant interpretive source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explained that most terms added/updated in this rule are not used in other standards cited by commenters; for those that are (e.g., gas and liquid in 29 CFR 1910.120 and 1926.1101), contextual usage in the other standards should make meaning clear. OSHA does not anticipate confusion but emphasized that specific guidance for other standards remains authoritative for interpreting those standards.
